query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy (HEA), a controlled thermomechanical treatment—such as a post-annealing aging step at an elevated temperature—accelerates the local diffusion of minor solutes to grain boundaries, leading to the nucleation of fine intermetallic precipitates that weaken the grain-boundary cohesion. This embrittlement mechanism differs from that in conventional alloys because, although the alloy retains its refined, single‐phase matrix (and suppresses rapid grain coarsening), the treatment is sufficient to trigger localized chemical inhomogeneities that reduce toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully single‐phase HEA with a homogeneous distribution of solutes and a fine-grained microstructure, exhibiting a balance of high toughness and ductility.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled thermomechanical treatment (e.g., specific annealing/aging cycle) designed to stimulate grain-boundary solute segregation without causing extensive grain growth.
generation.conditions: The treatment involves aging at an elevated temperature (close to, but below, the melting range) for a duration sufficient to permit noticeable diffusion yet short enough to avoid overall coarsening, followed by standard cooling to room temperature. Comparisons will be made between treated and untreated (baseline) samples under service-like loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, brittle intermetallic precipitates localized at grain boundaries as a result of solute segregation during the treatment.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature in the post-processing treatment enhances atomic mobility, causing minor solute species to migrate to grain boundaries where they nucleate fine precipitates. These precipitates reduce the cohesion of the boundaries, leading to embrittlement even though the overall single-phase structure and grain size remain largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, treated HEA samples will exhibit reduced toughness and ductility as measured by lower fracture energies and increased brittleness. This outcome will be observable despite the retention of a refined grain structure, distinguishing it from conventional alloy embrittlement where grain coarsening is prominent.
generation.baseline: Untreated, homogeneously single-phase HEA exhibiting robust ductility and toughness under similar loading and service conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected within the regime of service conditions where the designed thermomechanical treatment (temperature, time, and cooling rate) is applicable; extremes of very high temperature or very rapid loading might not trigger or might mask the subtle precipitate-driven embrittlement mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Exact kinetics of solute segregation and precipitate formation in HEAs under these conditions are not fully established; the magnitude of toughness reduction may vary with specific alloy composition and treatment parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples from the same batch. Subject one set to the defined controlled thermomechanical treatment (specific aging cycle) and leave the other set untreated as a baseline. Characterize both sets using high-resolution TEM and EDS to detect any grain-boundary precipitates. Perform standardized mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness and ductility assessments) under service-like loading conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM, EDS) to identify and quantify grain-boundary precipitates
Fracture toughness tests (e.g., using standard crack propagation methods)
Ductility and yield strength measurements via stress–strain testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If treated samples do not exhibit significant grain-boundary precipitate formation or if their mechanical properties (toughness and ductility) are statistically indistinguishable from those of the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis that the controlled thermomechanical treatment causes embrittlement via solute segregation would be falsified.
